title: Kelpware self-serve evaluation & time-to-first-token path
summary: Intro discovery for Kelpware evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Discussed quickstart (free credits), time-to-first-token (TTFT), security (SOC2, KMS, SSO), networking options (VPC, on-prem), and a follow-up benchmark pilot. SE offered micro-benchmark and sample curl/SDK examples; customer asked about KV cache, batching and cost/latency tradeoffs.
next_steps: Redwood to provision trial credits and test account
SE to run micro-benchmark using Kelpware sample dataset (end of next week)
Share security package (SOC2 report, KMS/HSM notes, SSO/SCIM guide)
Schedule technical deep dive for private deployment (tentatively 2026-06-17)
Send quickstart curl + SDK snippet and sample prompts
action_items: Alex Moreno: provision test account and invite Kelpware (due 2026-06-10)
Priya Shah: prepare micro-benchmark plan and sample Jupyter with instructions (due 2026-06-12)
Ravi Patel (Kelpware): share small sample dataset and expected p99 latency target (due 2026-06-11)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-08 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood SE), James (Kelpware CTO), Marisol (Head of ML), Ravi (Infra), Tara (PM)

[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros — I'm Alex, AE on the Redwood account team, with Priya and Liam from our solutions engineering team. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] James: Good, thanks. Quick agenda from our side, want to understand what it takes to get Kelpware from prototype to first production call. We have two main constraints: latency around 150ms p95 for small single-turn responses and strict data residency for EU-only data.
[00:00:22] Priya: Got it. We'll run through the self-serve quickstart, the hosted credits flow, and then outline options for Dedicated or Private if you need VPC/on-prem. We'll also call out security controls — SSO, KMS, audit logs.
[00:00:35] Marisol: Great. Also want to know effort to get to first token — we have a small ML infra team but want minimal ops at first.
[00:00:42] Liam: Totally reasonable. For most teams the TTFT is measured in hours if you use the hosted API and our quickstart templates. We'll show the curl snippet, node/python SDKs, and a small sample app.

[00:01:05] Alex: Before we dig in, can you remind us of your current stack? Are you hitting any blockers with huggingface endpoints or other providers?
[00:01:12] James: We're running internal prototypes on a mixture of open models hosted on our cluster — some quantized weights on NVidia A40s. But it's very brittle; our infra team spends more time on the orchestration than on building product value. We're evaluating Redwood mainly for operational simplicity and predictable cost.
[00:01:30] Ravi: And compliance: reg-driven customers require EU data at rest, and we need to control KMS keys. We didn't see a clear path with some public APIs.

[00:01:46] Priya: That's a common pattern. Hosted gives you fastest TTFT — we can create an account, grant free credits for you to test, and you can point requests to our hosted endpoint. If you need customer-managed keys and VPC, Dedicated or Private are options. Private will give you a customer-controlled control plane and on-prem packaging.
[00:02:05] Marisol: For hosted, how do you handle data retention? Do you use it for training?
[00:02:12] Priya: By default, hosted doesn't use customer content for model training and we have retention controls — you can opt into shorter retention windows or have it disabled for certain enterprise tiers. We'll share the exact retention policy in the security package.

[00:02:30] [00:02:30] Tara: And SSO — we use Okta. How's the SAML/SCIM integration?
[00:02:35] Alex: We support SAML SSO and SCIM user provisioning on enterprise tiers; we can enable SSO for your trial if you'd like to test RBAC flows.

[00:02:48] James: One of our big questions is cost vs latency. If we use the hosted API with larger models, costs can get high. What levers do you provide to control unit economics?
[00:02:58] Priya: We have a few levers: model selection (smaller model variants), dynamic routing to cheaper model variants for non-critical traffic, quantization profiles that maintain quality but lower cost, and automatic batching/caching. For prefix-heavy workloads we do KV caching which reduces repeated token compute — though there are consistency considerations for dynamic content.
[00:03:19] Ravi: When you say KV caching, is that prefix-only or do you support more generalizable caching? We worry about stale cache for personalized responses.
[00:03:27] Priya: Great question. The current system focuses on prefix/KV cache for repeated system prompts or instruction prefixes; for personalized content we recommend per-customer cache keys with short TTLs. Cache invalidation and fallbacks are part of the rollout playbook. We'll share docs with TTL recommendations.

[00:03:48] [00:03:48] James: For a first pilot, we'd likely run a small set of endpoints hitting typical user prompts — maybe 10k calls/day to measure cost and p95 latency. Can Redwood simulate expected throughput with your micro-benchmark?
[00:03:59] Liam: Yes. We can run a micro-benchmark using your sample payloads and sequence-length distributions. Priya will outline the exact steps but typically we run a few scenarios: steady load, spike to simulate burst, and real-world user prompt distribution.

[00:04:20] Marisol: Are these micro-benchmarks run on hosted infra or do you provision dedicated instances to mirror production?
[00:04:27] Priya: We can run on hosted and show what you'd see on our shared fleet; for a Dedicated evaluation we can spin up a reserved pool that matches the GPU type and memory profile. That gives you a clearer projection of per-token cost and p95/p99 latencies.

[00:04:45] Tara: Timeline — we need a pilot in our EU staging environment in the next three weeks. Is that feasible?
[00:04:52] Alex: Yes, provisioning a hosted trial with region-specific routing to EU is straightforward. For Dedicated or Private we might need lead time for reserved capacity or on-prem packaging, but that's typically a few weeks to coordinate.

[00:05:10] [00:05:10] James: Another specific: we do some streaming chat and tool-calling. Does Redwood support streaming tokens and function/tool calling patterns?
[00:05:18] Priya: Yes — streaming responses are first-class on the API and function/tool calling is supported. We also have structured output helpers and schema enforcement to reduce hallucinations in tool outputs.

[00:05:33] Ravi: Encryption keys — can we bring our own KMS? Our compliance team wants HSM-backed keys for anything persisted.
[00:05:40] Priya: For Dedicated and Private you can bring your own KMS/HSM. For hosted we support customer-managed keys in specific enterprise packages; we will include KMS notes in the security package.

[00:05:54] Alex: I'm going to demo the quickstart — very quick curl and SDK example to show TTFT. I'll share my screen.
[00:06:00] [screen share noise, short pause]
[00:06:10] Alex: (typing) Example curl: curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>' -d '{"model":"redwood-2-small","input":"Summarize the following..."}' — that's it. From account creation to first token we often see teams hit usable results in under an hour if they use the sample templates.

[00:06:40] James: Ok, that's encouraging. For Node and Python SDK are there code samples to wire up streaming?
[00:06:46] Liam: Yes, both SDKs support streaming with an event emitter pattern. We'll drop sample snippets in the quickstart repo.

[00:06:58] Marisol: Any gotchas with CORS or client-side usage? We sometimes want to do inference from client apps.
[00:07:04] Priya: We usually recommend routing through a backend to keep keys secure. If you do client calls we advise short-lived tokens with a strong proxy and rate limits. We'll include patterns in the playbook.

[00:07:20] [00:07:20] Ravi: For Private on-prem, what does deployment look like? Does the package require special interconnects or specific GPUs?
[00:07:28] Priya: The on-prem package is flexible — we support common enterprise GPUs (A100, H100, A40) and have a hardware compatibility matrix. Network-wise, the control plane can be customer-hosted and we support various connectivity options. We'll coordinate a deeper ops review if you decide to pursue Private.

[00:07:45] James: One more question: If we start hosted and later move to Dedicated, is model versioning and rollout preserved? We don't want to rework prompts and prompt templates across environments.
[00:07:55] Priya: Yes — our deployment abstraction keeps model versions and rollout policies consistent. You can pin model versions per-environment and use our rollouts (canary, A/B) with automatic fallback to a compatible variant. That helps keep prompts stable.

[00:08:12] Tara: What's a realistic timeline and resource plan for a three-week staged pilot?
[00:08:18] Alex: Proposed plan: week 0 — create hosted trial with credits and quickstart app; week 1 — micro-benchmark with Kelpware sample payload; week 2 — iterate on model selection, enable caching/batching config; week 3 — decision point to stay hosted for production or move to Dedicated/Private. We'll send a one-page runbook.

[00:08:41] [00:08:41] Marisol: We care about hallucination controls for certain workflows. Any eval tooling?
[00:08:47] Liam: We have an evals integration — you can run prompt-sets and track quality regressions over time. Optimize will also recommend quantization and batching profiles that preserve quality.

[00:09:05] James: On the security docs — can you pre-send SOC2 and any penetration test summaries?
[00:09:11] Alex: Absolutely. We'll attach SOC2 Type II, pen test summary, and our privacy and retention docs.

[00:09:20] Priya: Quick note on cost modeling: for 10k calls/day with average 120 tokens per call, we'll model both redwood-2-small and medium variants and show expected monthly cost estimates. We'll include both hosted and Dedicated projections.

[00:09:37] Ravi: Will you also show the delta if we enable KV cache and batching? We want to see the real savings.
[00:09:42] Priya: Yes — micro-benchmark will include baseline and cache-enabled runs. We'll also surface tail latency changes when batching is enabled vs single-example mode.

[00:09:58] [00:09:58] James: Any compliance certifications around EU data residency specifically?
[00:10:03] Alex: We host in EU regions and can restrict routing so data stays in EU for hosted customers. We'll share region details and our data residency commitments in the security package.

[00:10:20] Tara: For the trial account — what's the onboarding friction? Do we need lots of paperwork?
[00:10:25] Alex: For hosted trial it's minimal: sign-up, accept trial terms, and we provision credits. For enterprise features like SAML+KMS we may need an MSA or addendum; we'll surface that early.

[00:10:38] Marisol: Are there rate limits that will affect our pilot? We do spiky loads during certain hours.
[00:10:43] Liam: Hosted accounts have rate limits; we can temporarily raise limits for your pilot. For production at scale we'd recommend Dedicated reserved capacity to prevent throttling.

[00:10:55] [00:10:55] James: Okay, sounds good. Let's talk about acceptance criteria — what would Redwood consider a successful pilot?
[00:11:02] Alex: Typical success criteria: p95 latency under your target (150ms), cost per 1k tokens in expected budget, no major security blockers (SOC2, KMS acceptable), and integration with your auth flows. We'll align on exact KPIs in the email follow-up.

[00:11:20] Priya: I'll also include a short checklist for TTFT: create API keys, run sample calls, run streaming chat, run micro-benchmark, and review security docs.

[00:11:30] Tara: Great — talk to us about rollout strategies if we go Dedicated. How do upgrades and rollbacks work?
[00:11:37] Priya: Rollouts are supported with canary and A/B. If a new model or quantization variant underperforms, automatic fallback policies can route to a previous variant. We keep per-route dashboards and traces to quickly identify regressions.

[00:11:53] [00:11:53] James: Is observability included? We need per-route token-cost breakdown and tracing hooks to tie requests to our logs.
[00:11:59] Liam: Yes — the Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns, per-model dashboards, tracing integrations, and error analysis. You can also export traces into your existing telemetry.

[00:12:15] Ravi: One subtlety: we run a lot of short sequences under 64 tokens — will batching help or hurt latency?
[00:12:22] Priya: It depends on workload shape. For many short synchronous calls, batching can increase throughput and reduce cost with small latency penalty. We can tune autoscaling and batching windows to fit your p95 target. The micro-benchmark will quantify that for you.

[00:12:40] [00:12:40] Alex: Quick demo wrap-up — I'll drop the quickstart repo link and a one-click onboarding doc in chat.
[00:12:48] Alex: (chat link posted) https://app.redwood.ai/quickstart/kelpware-sample — that'll include a sample Jupyter and curl snippets.

[00:13:00] Marisol: Cool, I saw the link. We'll try the sample and hand over a small dataset for the benchmark.

[00:13:07] James: Final question — any special licensing or MSA language for Dedicated or Private?
[00:13:12] Alex: We have standard enterprise agreements; for Private on-prem there is a platform fee and support contract. We'll share a summary of commercial terms for your review.

[00:13:25] Tara: Ok, let's recap next steps.
[00:13:28] Alex: Recap: Redwood will provision a hosted trial and grant credits; Priya will draft micro-benchmark plan; we'll share SOC2 and KMS docs; Kelpware to share sample data and p95 target. We'll tentatively schedule a technical deep dive on 2026-06-17.

[00:13:45] James: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[00:13:48] Marisol: Thanks.
[00:13:50] Priya: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the runbook and links.

[00:13:55] [00:13:55] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: Some technical terms were transcribed imperfectly (e.g., "KV cash" instead of "KV cache", "SAML sp" clipped). There was occasional cross-talk and multiple people speaking at once; timestamps are approximate.
